title: B-Tree Indexes, EXPLAIN Query Plans & Avoiding Scans
summary: Understand leftmost prefix rules on composite indexes, non-sargable traps, partial indexes, and reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE node metrics cleanly.
learningObjectives: Order composite index columns cleanly by equality selectivity first, range filters second
Diagnose Sequential Scan bottlenecks using EXPLAIN ANALYZE and cure deep-offset slowdown via Keyset pagination
prerequisiteConcepts: Understanding of basic queries and tables

sections.heading: 1. How Composite B-Trees & Sargability Work
sections.content:
Every time SQL filters an unindexed column (`Seq Scan`), the database reads millions of disk pages scanning row by row (`O(n)`). Adding a **B-Tree index** sorts column pointers into a balanced tree enabling logarithmic `O(log n)` hops.

Two rules govern production indexing cleanly: **1. Column Ordering**: on a composite index `(tenant_id, created_at)`, queries filtering `tenant_id` alone OR `(tenant_id, created_at)` hit the index fast—filtering `created_at` ALONE misses it because the leftmost column comes first! **2. Sargability**: NEVER wrap indexed columns inside functions (`WHERE LOWER(email) = ...` or `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026`), or the engine abandons the B-Tree unless a matching expression index or clean range comparison is supplied.

codeExamples.code:
Unindexed:       SELECT ... OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 20  -> Discards 500,000 scanned rows! O(N)
Keyset Cursor:   WHERE created_at < $last_ts LIMIT 20 -> B-Tree jumps straight to cursor! O(log N)
codeExamples.explanation: Keyset seek pagination scales smoothly at page 100,000 while OFFSET degrades linearly across large tables.

keyPoints: Every secondary index speeds reads (`SELECT`) while costing extra disk storage and slightly slower writes (`INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE`)—don't over-index blindly!
Replace `OFFSET` with cursor/keyset pagination on infinite feeds and large admin logs.
commonMistakes: Using `SELECT *` everywhere instead of targeted projections, preventing Index-Only Scans!

sections.heading: 2. Inspecting EXPLAIN ANALYZE & Composite Index Creation
sections.content: Before shipping high-traffic endpoints, verify the optimizer hits `Index Scan` rather than `Seq Scan` via `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.

codeExamples.code:
-- Equality column FIRST ('status'), range/sort column SECOND ('created_at DESC')
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created
  ON orders (status, created_at DESC)
  WHERE status IN ('pending', 'processing');

-- Check actual plan execution metrics cleanly:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total_cents, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 25;
codeExamples.explanation: Equality columns leading composite partial indexes let PostgreSQL seek exact pending targets in sub-millisecond time.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Index Scan using idx_orders_status_created on orders (cost=... actual time=0.08..0.14ms rows=25)

keyPoints: Use partial indexes (`WHERE status = 'pending'`) to exclude millions of already-archived rows from index maintenance.
commonMistakes: Adding indexes without running `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in busy live Postgres production databases (which otherwise locks writes!).

exercises.title: Optimize Slow Pagination & Non-Sargable Date Filter
exercises.objective: Rewrite non-sargable queries cleanly and design an optimal composite index.
exercises.description: Refactor: `SELECT * FROM logs WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) = 2026 AND service_name = 'auth' ORDER BY created_at DESC OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 50;`
instructions: Rewrite `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM ...)` as an sargable explicit timestamp range (`>=` and `<`).
Design the ideal composite index column order `(service_name, created_at)`.
hints: Equality match (`service_name`) comes before range/order column (`created_at`).
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Explicit range conditions paired with `(service_name, created_at)` and cursor seek transform multi-second scans into sub-millisecond reads.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: On a composite index `ON events (org_id, created_at)`, which query cleanly utilizes the leftmost index order?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: B-Tree composite indexes sort primarily by the leftmost key (`org_id`), requiring it to match efficiently.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why does `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'alice@x.com'` skip a normal `INDEX(email)` unless configured specially?

options.text: Wrapping an indexed column in a function breaks sargability because the B-Tree stores raw original values, not lowercased hashes
Emails cannot be indexed in B-Trees

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Maintain canonical lowercase emails on write or create a matching expression index `ON users(LOWER(email))`.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on active production PostgreSQL tables?

options.text: Builds the index cleanly without acquiring write-blocking locks over live INSERT/UPDATE transactions
Skips B-Tree balancing to build instantaneously

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Standard index builds lock writes on busy tables for minutes/hours; concurrent creation avoids downtime.

recap: You mastered composite B-Tree design, sargable query rewrites, Keyset pagination, and EXPLAIN plan inspection.
